title: What will be the winning margin in Brazil’s 2026 presidential election runoff?
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the difference, in percentage points of valid votes, between the first- and second-place candidates in the Brazlian national presidential election held on October 25, 2026, published by Brazil’s [Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE)](https://www.tse.jus.br/eleicoes/informacoes-tecnicas-sobre-a-divulgacao-de-resultados).

The value will be calculated as: winner’s valid-vote share − runner-up’s valid-vote share. For example, if the winner receives 52.4% of valid votes and the runner-up receives 47.6%, the question resolves to 4.8 percentage points.
fine_print: [The TSE](https://www.tse.jus.br/comunicacao/noticias/2026/Marco/eleicoes-2026-confira-as-principais-datas-do-calendario-eleitoral) defines valid votes as votes cast for candidates, excluding blank and null ballots. The final nationwide TSE presidential result will be used including any corrected official figures.
background:
Brazil held the first round of its 2026 general election on October 4, 2026. No presidential candidate won an absolute majority of valid votes. With t[he vast majority of the votes counted](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-race-election-result-second-round-lula-flavio-bolsonaro) the President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won 45.1% (53.8m votes) whilst his Liberal Party challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro won 47.0% (56.1m votes). The second-round runoff will be held on October 25, 2026.

The presidential contest is forecasted to be highly competitve. The victory margin can imply very different political environments irrespective of the eventual winner. The runoff margin can therefore serve as a compact indicator of electoral polarization, the breadth of the eventual winner’s coalition, and the degree to which the electorate remains evenly divided at the end of the campaign.

A [Datafolha poll](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/lula-maintains-lead-over-flavio-bolsonaro-ahead-brazil-election-datafolha-poll-2026-09-17/) on September 17 reported Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 44% in a hypothetical second-round matchup, while [other recent polls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_polling_for_the_2026_Brazilian_presidential_election) have also shown narrow margins and variation in which candidate holds a numerical lead. The runoff margin can move materially during the remaining campaign because of candidate debates, endorsements, economic news, campaign strategy, first-round vote transfers, and changes in turnout among different voter blocs.

comments.author: VectorWright
comments.text:
Going with a point estimate around 4.0, not far off the current 3.78, with a slightly wider interval than what's up there now.



The most relevant data point is Datafolha's first runoff survey (Oct 6-7, n\=2,520, +/-2pt MoE), which has Flavio at 52-48 among valid votes, or 49-45 overall. That's about a 4 point gap, basically the same direction and magnitude the community's already pricing in. Quaest's 44-42 number is older, from before the first round, so I'm weighting Datafolha higher here.



What makes me want the tails a bit wider than the current 2.35-5.3: this same electorate just handed pollsters a surprise in the first round. Bolsonaro beat his pre-election numbers by several points while Lula underperformed his. One poll miss doesn't mean round two is guaranteed to miss too, but it's a reason not to trust a tight interval off a single post-first-round survey.



Both key factors already flagged here, third-way vote transfers and right-wing congressional gains, point the same direction as the polling move. I don't see a reason to fight that consensus, just widen the uncertainty band a little given how fresh and thin the second-round polling still is.

comments.text: @(tejvn)There are two parts. First, the flatness of the distribution near zero is tied to the implied win probabilities. I have Lula lower than you do so my forecast is not as flat as yours, and it's fine. Basically, any shape is ok as long as it reflects the forecaster's beliefs about the candidates' chances. However, any forecast assigning a meaningful probability to Lula must be asymmetrical, so any distribution that looks symmetrical but has a significant cutoff at zero is wrong. That's the problem with the community forecast right now.

comments.author: tejvn
comments.text:
The community prediction underestimates the probability mass between 0% and 2%. Furthermore, any smooth forecast should be flat at x \= 0%.

### Why The Distribution "Folds" at x \= 0%

This question resolves as the absolute value of the vote-share difference rather than the signed difference of the vote share itself. This is equivalent to the signed-distribution folded back onto itself at x \= 0%. In practice, this would take two components. The main component corresponds to a win by Flavio, the frontrunner (85% mass), and the second component corresponds to Lula winning (15% mass). At x \= 0, the two components should meet at equal height with opposite slopes. The combined distribution should then have zero slope at x \= 0 instead of the left tail tapering downwards, which puts noticeably more mass in the 0–2% range than the current community forecast does.

### PDF

![](https://cdn.metaculus.com/user_uploaded/Screenshot_2026-10-08_at_10.14.21PM.png)

### Appendix (Proof for Math Nerds)

Assume that the probability distribution function for the signed difference in vote-share, $V(x)$, is continuously differentiable. The distribution for the absolute difference should be $A(x) = V(x) + V(-x)$ defined for $x \ge 0$. Therefore, $A(0) = V(0) + V(-0) = 2V(0)$, and

$$
\lim_{x \to 0^+} A'(x) = V'(0) - V'(0) = 0.
$$

This proof breaks down if your forecast for the signed difference, $V(x)$, is not continuously differentiable, however this argument is, in my opinion, irrelevant given that there over a hundred million voters.
